text:
[EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]

T he first half National Government Budget Implementation Review Report covers 1 st July to 31 st  December 2025 and is the second report for FY 2025/26. The report has been prepared to comply with Article 228(6) of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit quarterly budget implementation reports to Parliament for the National and County governments.

The FY 2025/26 is the third budget under the fourth Medium-Term Plan (MTP) (2023-2027) of the Kenya Vision 2030 and is being implemented under the Bottom-up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) framework. Under this framework, the government aims to achieve economic turnaround and inclusive growth by increasing investments in at least five sectors that significantly impact the economy and household welfare. These sectors include Agricultural Transformation, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Housing and Settlement, Healthcare, Digital Superhighway, and Creative Industry. The agenda also focuses on increasing employment, equitable income distribution, and social security, while expanding the tax base and boosting foreign exchange earnings.

The FY 2025/26 is the third budget under the fourth Medium-Term Plan (MTP) (2023-2027) of the Kenya Vision 2030 and is being implemented under the Bottom-up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) framework. Under this framework, the government aims to achieve economic turnaround and inclusive growth by increasing investments in at least five sectors that significantly impact the economy and household welfare. These sectors include Agricultural Transformation, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Housing and Settlement, Healthcare, Digital Superhighway, and Creative Industry. The agenda also focuses on increasing employment, equitable income distribution, and social security, while expanding the tax base and boosting foreign exchange earnings.

The National Government's original gross budget for FY 2025/26 was Kshs.4.69 trillion, compared to Kshs.4.37 trillion for FY 2024/25. This comprises Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, which was 16 per cent of the original gross national budget and 29 per cent of the original gross ministerial budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Recurrent allocation comprised the ministerial recurrent allocation of Kshs.1.80 trillion (38 per cent of the original gross national budget) and Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) at Kshs.2.14 trillion (46 per cent of the original gross national budget). Notably, the Education Sector received the highest budget allocation of Kshs.703.07 billion, followed by Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communication Technology Kshs.534.63 billion, reflecting their key role in the economy.

text:
[EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]

In the first six months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed to ensure seamless budget implementation not only in the current financial year but also for posterity. These included low absorption of the development budget, incomplete automation of the procurement and exchequer processes for National Government entities, and an upsurge in the use of Supplementary Budget under Article 223 of the Constitution for withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund.

The upsurge in the use of Article 223 of the Constitution in the first six months was mainly towards other operating expenses and the buyback of an International Sovereign Bond. The Controller of Budget approved Kshs.115.11 billion, comprising Kshs.8.66 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.106.44 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing 2 per cent of the gross estimates. Of the total exchequer issues under Article 223 of the Constitution, issuance of an International sovereign bond for liability management operations in the FY2025/2026 received Kshs.86.29 billion, representing 75 per cent of the total requests.

To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends collaboration of all Stakeholders in the implementation of the Electronic Government Procurement System, including its integration with IFMIS, training of users, both staff and suppliers and technical support to fast-track procurement of the planned activities. Also, the National Treasury should automate the exchequer process for all the votes to foster efficiency and effectiveness in budget implementation.

Further, the Controller of Budget recommends adopting sound planning, budget practices, and effective expenditure management by prioritising essential services and aligning them with operational realities during budget formulation and implementation. This will reduce the use of Article 223 of the Constitution on budget items that were foreseeable during the budget process and could not be accommodated during the sector working groups due to resource constraints. Good budget implementation practices will enhance fiscal responsiveness, ensuring accountability and budget credibility.

text:
[1.  INTRODUCTION]

T he Controller of Budget prepared this report in fulfilment of Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of the budgets of the national and county governments.

This report is in line with Section 9(2) of the Controller of Budget Act Cap 429, which outlines the information to be reported by the Controller of Budget in the quarterly budget implementation reports. In addition, it is aligned with Section 9(5) of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which states that, despite the first quarterly report submitted under Section 9, each subsequent report shall contain cumulative amounts from the beginning of that year. To meet the legal requirements governing the content of budget implementation review reports, the report is presented in seven chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter two presents the performance of receipts into the Consolidated Fund and Exchequer Issues to Ministries, Departments and Agencies, Consolidated Fund Services and the County Revenue Fund as part of the equitable share of revenue to the forty-seven counties. Exchequer issues performance is expressed as a percentage of the annual net estimates.

Chapter Three presents the overall budget performance of the national government, including performance under the Consolidated Fund Services, Ministerial expenditure by economic classification, and the stock of Trade Payables (pending bills) for national government entities.   Chapter Four presents the budget performance of the eighty-seven MDAs clustered into ten Sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, which is planned to support fiscal analysis by breaking down government fiscal statistics for comparability. It presents the approved budget referred to as the gross estimates, accrued expenditure, which is further disaggregated into programme and sub-programmes performance and project implementation for MDAs. The absorption rate, which measures the performance, is calculated as a proportion of expenditure relative to the annual budget.

text:
[2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund]

The Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes monies reasonably exempted by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose, or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. Notably, at the beginning of FY 2023/24, the government directed that all fees collected by national government entities for services be deposited into the e-citizen account under Paybill number 222222.

To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted various revenue sources to raise funds. The sources include Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.63 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.127.65 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.1.10 trillion - comprising net domestic borrowing of Kshs.634.75 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.463.51 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.561.81 billion), and other domestic financing (Kshs.10.80 billion). The Government also targeted to raise Kshs.672 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.334.26 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.337.74 billion development A-I-A.

[2.3.  Net Exchequer Issues by the National Treasury]

Net exchequer issues refer to actual issues from the Consolidated Fund and Equalization Fund to MDAs and County Governments by the National Treasury, excluding Appropriations in Aid.

In the first six months of FY 2025/2026, net exchequer issues to National and County governments amounted to Kshs.2.14 trillion, representing 48 per cent of the revised annual net estimates, compared to Kshs.1.71 trillion (40 per cent) issued in a similar period of FY 2024/2025.

Table 2.2 summarises exchequer issues by the National Treasury in the first six months of FY 2025/2026.

Source: National Treasury & OCOB

Analysis in Table 2.2 shows that the Recurrent vote recorded the highest percentage of exchequer issues to revised net estimates, at 51 per cent. In contrast, the Ministerial Development vote recorded the lowest, at 36 per cent.

CFS vote received the highest proportion of exchequer issues to the total issues at 50 per cent, while the ministerial development vote received the lowest at 2 per cent. Figure 2.3 illustrates the proportion of exchequer issues by major category in the first six months of FY 2025/2026.

[2.4.  Exchequer Issues by Sector.]

MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the Classification of Functions of Government (COFOG), which is designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability across sectors.

The ten sectors are (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development, (ii) Education (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations and (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation.

In the first six months of FY 2025/2026, exchequer issues to MDAs amounted to Kshs.954.23 billion, representing 51 per cent of the original annual net estimates of Kshs.4.02 trillion, compared to 47 per cent (Kshs.784.36 billion) recorded in a similar period of FY 2024/2025. Table 2.3 summarises the sector's exchequer issues in the first six months of FY 2025/2026.

Source: National Treasury

The Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector received the highest proportion of exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 61 per cent, which is attributed to high proportions of exchequer transfers to the State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs and the State Department for Children Welfare Services at 76 per cent and 52 per cent, respectively.

[2.4.5  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution]

Article 223 of the Constitution allows the national government to access additional funding during the budget implementation by spending money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need for unbudgeted expenditure arises for which no amount has been appropriated, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund.

The total approved additional funding by the Cabinet Secretary, National Treasury, amounted to Kshs.177.46 billion, comprising Kshs.45.06 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.132.42 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing 4 per cent of the gross national budget. This was within the Constitutional threshold of ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament in any particular financial year (Kshs.4.69 trillion for FY 2025/26) in line with Article 223(5) of the Constitution.

In the first six months of FY 2025/2026, exchequer issues pursuant to Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya was Kshs.115.11 billion, comprising Kshs.8.66 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.106.45 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing 2 per cent of the annual gross estimates, compared to 0.04 per cent (Kshs.16.95 billion), issued in a similar period of FY2024/2025.

[2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund]

The Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund to provide only essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.

In the first six months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget authorised 12 requests amounting to Kshs.1.11 billion from the Equalization Fund. The amount comprised Kshs.68.16 million for Policy 1 development pending bills in favour of the Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Kshs.955.37 million for the Second Policy development projects in 13 County Governments.

[3.3.2  Overdraft Facility]

The overdraft facility is a short-term borrowing facility for the Government to cover temporary cash shortfalls. It is repayable within twelve months. Kenya's Government overdraft is administered by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). It is restricted to a maximum of five percent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.

In the period under review, the overdraft limit stood at Kshs.97.05 billion and was charged an average interest rate of 9.41 per cent per annum on the amount outstanding at the end of each month. In the first six months of FY 2025/2026, the total charge on the overdraft facility was Kshs.1.58 billion, as shown in Table 3.6.

Source: National Treasury

The decline in overdraft interest payments during the reporting period, compared to a similar period in FY 2024/25, was primarily due to implementation of the Treasury Single Account (TSA) System that commenced in July 2025 and a drop in CBK's interest rates, which stood at 9 per cent in December 2025, down from 11.25 per cent in December 2024.

[4.1.   Introduction]

MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. The chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in the first six months of FY 2025/2026. It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. The chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes and spending on development projects in the first six months of FY 2025/2026.

Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.

In FY 2025/2026, the Education Sector was allocated Kshs.703.07 billion, recording the highest budget allocation, attributed to its broad mandate, including primary schools, secondary schools, special education, tertiary education, university education, examinations and curriculum development, and reforms in the education sector. Conversely, the General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector received Kshs.58.16 billion, representing the lowest budgetary allocation.

text:
[4.2.1  Introduction]

Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030. The ARUD Sector comprises five sub-sectors, namely: The State Department for Lands and Physical Planning; the State Department for Livestock Development; the State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries; the State Department for Agriculture; and the National Land Commission (NLC), together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) and Training Institutions.

The Sector is a significant player in the delivery of national development agendas, namely, Kenya Vision 2030, the government plan -the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (2022-27), the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy, among other national and international policies and obligations. During the MTEF period 2025/26-2027/28, the sector plans to implement programmes that facilitate food and nutrition security, agro-processing, employment creation, and the utilisation of the blue economy.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

[4.3.1  Introduction]

The Education Sector comprises five MDAs: the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training, the State Department for Higher Education, the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research, the State Department for Basic Education, and the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), and their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.

The Sector envisions attaining 'Quality and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development' in Kenya. The Sector's strategic objectives include enhancing access, equity, quality and relevance in education, training and research; establishing, maintaining and managing professional teaching and learning services for all early learning centres, primary, secondary and tertiary institutions; enhancing development capacities for Science Technology and Innovations; enhance mechanisms for dissemination and commercialisation of research findings; improve data quality and sharing in education, training, research and labour market; promote vibrant industry - institutional linkages in the area of skilling for employability; and integrate ICT in Education, Training and Research for management, teaching and learning at all levels.

It is worth noting that the 2-6-3-3 system requires substantial infrastructure, equipment, and human capital in the medium term, from 2025/26 to 2027/28.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[4.3.2  Budget Performance for the Education Sector]

The  budgetary  allocation  to  Education  in  FY  2025/2026  amounted  to  Kshs.703.07  billion,  compared  to Kshs.681.98 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 15 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 28 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation included Kshs.29.78 billion (4 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.673.29 billion (96 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The Teachers Service Commission received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.387.18 billion (55 per cent of the Education Sector's budget), while the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 0.99 billion (0.1 per cent of the Education Sector allocation).

The high allocation to the Teachers Service Commission is attributed to its vital role in the Teacher Resource Management programme.  Figure 4.3 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Education Sector from FY 2021/2022 to FY 2025/2026.

Source: National Treasury

The total exchequer issues to the Education Sector amounted to Kshs. 356.74 billion, representing 57 per cent of the Sector's annual net estimates. This amount comprised Kshs.8.17 billion for development expenditure, representing 35 per cent of the annual development net estimates, and Kshs.348.57 billion for recurrent activities, representing 58 per cent of the annual recurrent net estimates.

[4.3.7  The Teachers Service Commission]

The Teachers Service Commission is mandated to formulate policies that regulate the teaching profession and guide teacher management functions, thereby ensuring compliance with the teaching standards prescribed from time to time. It also facilitates teachers' career progression and professional development, and monitors

their  conduct  and  performance during curriculum implementation. TSC registers trained teachers and recruits, employs, and assigns teachers employed by the commission. It further exercises disciplinary controls over registered teachers, terminates the employment of teachers, reviews the standards of education and training for persons entering the teaching service, reviews the demand for and supply of teachers, and advises the national government on matters related to the teaching profession.

This Sector consists of nine MDAs: the State Department for Roads, Transport, Shipping and Maritime Affairs; Housing and Urban Development; Public Works; Information, Communications Technology and Digital Economy; Broadcasting and Telecommunications; Energy; and Petroleum.

The EI&ICT Sector plays a vital role as an enabler of the country's socio-economic development. It is a crucial sector in realising Vision 2030 and the BETA Agenda.

[4.4.4  The State Department for Transport]

The State Department for Transport promotes the management of transport policy; manage rail transport and infrastructure; fast track identified northern and LAPPSET transport corridor projects; oversight and co-ordi-

text:
[4.5.1  Introduction]

The Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPWNR) Sector comprises six MDAs: State Departments for Environment and Climate Change; Forestry; Water and Sanitation; Irrigation; Wildlife; and Mining. The Sector also includes several autonomous and semi-autonomous government agencies. In addition, it

comprises the following entities: the National Environment Complaint Committee, the National Environment Tribunal, the Hydrologists Registration Board, and the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya.

The goal of the Sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment, with various objectives, including enhancing climate change resilience and reducing carbon emissions, improving the utilisation of land through irrigation and land reclamation, and promoting equitable and sustainable use of wildlife resources. The Sector plays a pivotal role in securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment, Kenya's natural capital, water provision, and generating foreign exchange for the country.

text:
[4.7.1  Introduction]

The Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector consists of seventeen MDAs, which include the State Department for Correctional Services; the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services; the National Police Service; the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration; the State Law Office; the Judiciary; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC); the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP); the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP); the Witness Protection Agency (WPA); the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNHCR); the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC); the Judicial Service Commission (JSC); the National Police Service Commission (NPSC); the National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC); the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) and the State Department for Justice, Human Rights and Constitutional Affairs, as well as SAGAs and tribunals each with specific functions and mandates.

The Sector creates a conducive environment for the country's economic, social, and political development, which is necessary for fulfilling the objectives of Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption. It is focused on strengthening the rule of law, democracy, and human rights through various functions such as public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, and the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.

text:
[4.7.1  Introduction]

The Sector creates a conducive environment for the country's economic, social, and political development, which is necessary for fulfilling the objectives of Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption. It is focused on strengthening the rule of law, democracy, and human rights through various functions such as public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, and the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.

This Sector is also responsible for developing and implementing citizenship and refugee management and immigration services, regulating the gaming industry, providing population management, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, conducting crime research, printing government documents, and overseeing policing.

source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

This amount comprised Kshs.4.32 billion for development expenditure, representing 49 per cent of development net estimates, and Kshs.133.29 billion for recurrent activities, representing 51 per cent of recurrent net estimates.

text:
[4.8.1  Introduction]

Health is primarily a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. The health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care at the national level. The sector comprises two MDAs: The State Department for Medical Services and the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards. The Sector delivers services through several SAGAs and entities, including the Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Syndemic Disease Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya and the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority.

The Sector envisions 'a healthy, productive and globally competitive nation, ' achieved through strategic objectives under equity, efficiency, and people-centred principles, with a multi-sectoral approach, as outlined in the Kenya Health Policy (2014-2030). The Health Sector implements its strategic objectives through eight budgetary programmes, four under the State Department for Medical Services and four under the State Department for Public Health and Professionals.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[4.8.2  Budget Performance for the Health Sector]

The budget allocation to the Health Sector in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.138.11 billion, compared to Kshs.135.19 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 3 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 5 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation includes Kshs.27.50 billion (20 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.110.61 billion (80 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Medical Services received the highest budget allocation of Kshs.105.95 billion (77 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards was allocated Kshs.32.15 billion (23 per cent of the Health Sector allocation).

The high allocation to the State Department for Medical Services was due to a large budget for the National Referral Services sub-programme. Figure 4.13 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Health Sector from FY 2021/2022 to FY 2025/2026.

text:
[4.10.1  Introduction]

The Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) sector consists of twenty-three MDAs, namely The Executive Office of the President, Office of the Deputy President, Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, State Department for National Government Coordination, State Department for Parliamentary Affairs, State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State Department for Special Programmes; State House; State Department for Devolution; State Department of Economic Planning; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; The National Treasury; State Department for Public Investments and Assets Management; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Senate; The Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA); Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; The Auditor General; The Controller of Budget, and The Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) together with affiliated SAGAs and entities.

The Sector provides national leadership, oversight, and policy direction towards realising the country's development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector, coordinates national and sectoral development planning, and oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.

The sector has prioritised  programmes and projects aligned with the Post-COVID-19 Economic Recovery Stimulus Programme (PC-ERS), the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, and the Fourth Medium Term Plan of Kenya Vision 2030. Priority was also accorded to ongoing interventions supporting the 'Big Four' agenda and the newly established institutions.

text:
[4.11.1  Introduction]

The Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector comprises seven MDAs: the State Departments for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy, Sports, Children Welfare Services, Culture, The Arts and Heritage, Labour and Skills Development, Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs, and Gender and Affirmative Action.

The strategic roles played by the Sector in the country's transformation and socio-economic development include Promoting and supporting youth empowerment and development; strengthening youth mainstreaming in  all  sectors;  spearheading  the  management  of  youth  policy  and  legislations;  promoting  engagement  with youth for national development; promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, and productive workforce; promotion of gender equity and equality; empowerment of communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights; and advancement of diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

[4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector]

The budget allocation to SPCR in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.78.99 billion, compared to Kshs.83.93 billion allocated in the previous financial year, 2024/2025. This amount represents 2 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation comprises Kshs.24.85 billion (31 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.54.15 billion (69 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.29.32 billion (37 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.3.59 billion (5 per cent of the SPCR Sector allocation).

cent of the original development net estimates, and Kshs. 32.88 billion for recurrent activities, representing 66 per cent of annual recurrent net estimates.

text:
[5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS]

In the first six months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that hampered budget implementation and made recommendations to address them. These issues included Low absorption of the development budget, as discussed below.
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget]

Observation: In  the  first  six  months  of  FY  2025/26,  the  national  government's  total  expenditure  was Kshs.2,183.86 billion, representing 47 per cent of the annual gross budget. This comprised ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.276.92 billion (absorption rate of 37 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure of Kshs.899.74 billion (absorption rate of 50 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services, Kshs.1,007.20 billion (absorption rate of 47 per cent).

The government directed the mandatory use of the Electronic Government Procurement System (E-GPs) by all public procuring entities, effective July 1 st, 2025, for the procurement of goods and services.   The e-GPS has posed challenges to the procurement process due to a steep learning curve for both MDAs staff and suppliers, integration issues with internal systems, and technical support problems that impact efficiency, competitiveness, and timely service delivery.   Overall, the challenges resulted in a delayed procurement process and, consequently, low absorption of the development budget.

Recommendation: The Controller of Budget recommends a collaborative effort by all stakeholders in implementing the E-GPs system. This includes integration with IFMIS, training staff and suppliers in its use and technical support by timely troubleshooting issues reported.
heading_path: 5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[5.2.  Automation of Exchequer Process]

Observations: The National Treasury, in liaison with the Central Bank of Kenya and the Office of the Controller of Budget, successfully rolled out exchequer automation for the National Government except for the Public Debt, the Judiciary, County governments, second-level from County Revenue Fund to County Operational Account, Equalization Fund and some specific votes for recurrent. The Controller of Budget acknowledges the progress made in the automation process and the ongoing processes to board all the government entities.

Recommendations: To enhance efficiency and effectiveness in the approval of withdrawals from public funds, the Controller of Budget recommends automating all votes to foster efficiency and effectiveness in budget implementation. This will also add to gains on the implementation of the Treasury Single Account.
heading_path: 5.2.  Automation of Exchequer Process
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution]

Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya provides for Supplementary appropriation for the national government to spend money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need has arisen for expenditure for a purpose for which no amount has been appropriated by that Act, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund. The approval of Parliament for any spending under this Article shall be sought within two months after the first withdrawal of the money, subject to clause (3). Clause 5 specifies that in any particular financial year, the national government may not spend under this Article more than ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament for that finan-

cial year unless, in exceptional circumstances, Parliament has approved a higher percentage.

In the first Half of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget has recorded an upsurge in requests for approval to release exchequer under Article 223 of the Constitution. A total of Kshs.115.11 billion was approved, comprising Public debt repayments (Kshs.86.29 billion), ministerial recurrent expenditure (Kshs.20.16 billion) and development expenditure (Kshs.8.66 billion).
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution]

In the first Half of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget has recorded an upsurge in requests for approval to release exchequer under Article 223 of the Constitution. A total of Kshs.115.11 billion was approved, comprising Public debt repayments (Kshs.86.29 billion), ministerial recurrent expenditure (Kshs.20.16 billion) and development expenditure (Kshs.8.66 billion).

Comparatively, the withdrawals under Article 223 of the Constitution in just the first half of FY 2025/2026 surpassed full year utilization of this Article in the past three financial years. In FY 2024/25, the Cabinet Secretary of the National Treasury granted approvals of funding requests amounting to Kshs.83.96 billion, out of which the total of Kshs.66.54 billion (2 per cent) was withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund. Similarly, in FY 2023/2024 approvals by the Cabinet Secretary amounted to Kshs.30.66 billion out of which Kshs.19.12 billion (less than 1 per cent) was withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund. Further, cumulative withdrawals under Article 223 for FY 2022/2023 totalled Kshs.69.20 billion (2 per cent).

In many instances, these withdrawals under Article 223 were for regular operations and the settlement of pending bills, which clearly demonstrate the existing weaknesses in the budgeting cycle. Increased use of Article 223 is likely to circumvent the budget process and credibility.

text:
[6.1.1  Status of Domestic Debt Stock, as at 31 st  December 2025]

Total public and publicly guaranteed debt has been on the rise over the years. The increase is driven by annual borrowing by the national government to finance the budget deficit and also to obtain additional funds to pay accumulated interest on the debt stock carried over from previous years. The public debt stock increased from Kshs.11,799.66 billion (67.8 percent of GDP) in June 2025 to Kshs.12,287.58 billion in December 2025. The fiscal deficit at the beginning of the FY 2024/25 was Kshs 1,010 billion (5.8 percent of GDP) and is expected to reduce to Kshs. 876.10 billion (4.5 percent of GDP) according to the 2026 Budget Policy Statement (BPS).

As at December 2025, domestic debt stock was Kshs.6,825.61 billion, an increase from Kshs.6,311.20 billion, as of 30 th June 2025, while the external debt stock decreased to Kshs. 5,461.97 billion, from Kshs. 5,488.46 billion in June 2025. Borrowing from the domestic market is undertaken primarily through Treasury Bills and Bonds, comprising 97.5 percent of the total domestic debt, an indicator that other elements of domestic debt, such as the Central Bank overdraft to the national government, constitute only a small proportion of the domestic debt. While domestic borrowing contributes positively to the development of the domestic debt market, increased borrowing leads to high domestic interest rates, which in turn lead to reduced investment due to the high cost of borrowing, crowding out private sector investments. Table 6.1 shows the composition of domestic debt as 31 st  December 2025.

text:
[6.2.  Domestic Debt Budget Performance]

In the first half of FY 2025/26, the total domestic debt payment was Kshs.545.90 billion, consisting of Kshs.183.66 billion and Kshs.362.24 billion for principal and interest payments, respectively. The total revenue collected during the same period was Kshs.1,243.40 billion, indicating 44 percent of the revenue was used to service domestic debt. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) recommends a threshold for total debt service (both domestic and external debt service) to revenue of 30 per cent, indicating that Kenya's debt service costs on domestically borrowed funds alone exceed the IMF-recommended threshold for overall debt by 14.13 percent. The high debt service costs can be attributed to high interest payments on Treasury bills and bonds. High debt service leads to a reduction in total revenues as funds collected from taxes are used to service the debt. When a high proportion of the collected revenues are used to service debt, it limits the ability of the government to implement other programmes and offer services to the public. This situation underscores the challenges faced by the government in managing its debt obligations while striving to maintain fiscal sustainability.
heading_path: 6.2.  Domestic Debt Budget Performance
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[6.3.  Recommendations]

To effectively manage the high domestic borrowing and the associated high interest rates, the government may consider the following:

Put in measures to reduce the fiscal deficit in the medium term in line with the projections of the 2025 Budget Policy Statement.

Aim to implement the provisions of the 2025 Medium-Term Debt Strategy that recommends a borrowing mix of 50:50 for domestic to external borrowing. This will reduce the over-reliance on domestic borrowing.

The government's 2025 Medium-Term Debt Strategy (MTDS) aimed to reduce reliance on short-term debt instruments like Treasury Bills and lengthen the maturity profile of public debt. This strategy is designed to mitigate refinancing risks and ensure debt sustainability.

The government may implement appropriate monetary policies to ensure a reduction in the domestic interest rates. The government should ensure that the adopted policies provide a conducive environment for the private sector to operate.
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

text:
[7. CONCLUSION]

The National Government Budget Implementation Review Report is prepared in fulfillment of Article 228(6) of the Constitution, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit a report on the implementation of budgets for national and county governments to each House of Parliament every four months. It provides an overview of financial and non-financial information on budget performance for the first six months of FY 2025/26 in line with Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which outlines the information to be published in the report. These included actual receipts into the Consolidated Fund, approved budget, funds released, total expenditure and project implementation.

Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.2.17 trillion, representing 49 per cent of the annual target. The Controller of Budget approved withdrawals of Kshs.2.15 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 48 per cent of the net annual estimates. Ministries, Departments and Agencies received Kshs.954.23 billion, representing 51 per cent of the net annual estimates, comprising Kshs.145.03 billion for ministerial development expenditure (36 per cent of the net annual estimates) and Kshs.809.19 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure (55 per cent of the net annual estimates). Consolidated Fund Services received Kshs.1.02 trillion, and County Governments received Kshs.172.23 billion as an equitable share of revenues raised nationally, representing 48 per cent and 42 per cent of the annual net estimates, respectively.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

text:
[7. CONCLUSION]

Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.2.17 trillion, representing 49 per cent of the annual target. The Controller of Budget approved withdrawals of Kshs.2.15 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 48 per cent of the net annual estimates. Ministries, Departments and Agencies received Kshs.954.23 billion, representing 51 per cent of the net annual estimates, comprising Kshs.145.03 billion for ministerial development expenditure (36 per cent of the net annual estimates) and Kshs.809.19 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure (55 per cent of the net annual estimates). Consolidated Fund Services received Kshs.1.02 trillion, and County Governments received Kshs.172.23 billion as an equitable share of revenues raised nationally, representing 48 per cent and 42 per cent of the annual net estimates, respectively.

The Gross accrued expenditure for the National Government in the period under review was Kshs.2.18 trillion, representing an absorption rate of 47 per cent, comprising ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.276.92 billion (absorption rate of 37 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure of Kshs.899.74 billion (absorption rate of 50 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.1.01 trillion (absorption rate of 47 per cent). The absorption was within the prorated target of 50 per cent in the first six months, except the ministerial development budget, which was at 37 per cent.

While overseeing budget implementation in the first six months of the financial year, the Controller of Budget identified Key issues and recommended how they should be addressed to enhance effective budget implementation. These included: low absorption of development budget, Automation of the exchequer process and Use of Supplementary Budget under Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION
source_file: NGBIRR for First-Six Months of FY 2025-26.pdf

text:
[7. CONCLUSION]

While overseeing budget implementation in the first six months of the financial year, the Controller of Budget identified Key issues and recommended how they should be addressed to enhance effective budget implementation. These included: low absorption of development budget, Automation of the exchequer process and Use of Supplementary Budget under Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes.

The Controller of Budget appreciates the government directive to roll out the Electronic Procurement System aimed at enhancing transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources. The teething challenges facing the process have been identified, and we recommend a timely address to hasten the procurement process and subsequent implementation of the development programmes.

The Controller of Budget recommends that the national government, through the National Treasury, fast-track automation of the exchequer process for all Votes, the Public Debt, the Equalization Fund and level two transfer of funds from the County Revenue Fund to County Operations Accounts for the County governments. This will reduce turnaround time and ensure timely approval of withdrawals from public funds and the timely delivery of services.

On the issues of Supplementary Estimates under Article 223 of the Constitution, the Controller of Budget recommends a review of the legislative framework to provide for clear criteria for funding under Article 223 and the mechanisms for controls to ensure fiscal integrity and safeguard budget transparency.

Finally, regarding the increase in domestic debt, the Controller of Budget recommends government intervention to avert adverse effects emanating from over-reliance on domestic borrowing to meet the budget deficit.
